title: Windows Support 1: Desktop & Access Essentials
subject: File Permissions & Client Management
description: Step into the shoes of a Tier 1 Support Tech. Solve everyday tickets involving NTFS, file systems, and domain connectivity using an evidence-first workflow.
reportOverview: This report evaluates your ability to troubleshoot user-facing issues. Key skills tested: NTFS vs Share permissions, Active Directory group membership, and file system architecture.
evidenceInstructions:
Instructions:
1) Read the user's complaint.
2) Use the initial step to gather evidence.
3) Diagnose the logic error.
4) Apply the Fix and review the Resolution Insight to see why your solution worked.

tickets.title: HR New Hire Access Request
tickets.summary: Sarah in HR cannot open the 'HR_Private' folder. Other HR staff have no issues. You've confirmed she is in the 'HR_Department' group.

triage.q: What is the most efficient way to see exactly why Sarah is being blocked?
options: Check 'Effective Access' for sjenkins on the folder

diagnosis.q: Sarah is in 'HR_Department', but the folder allows 'HR_Staff'. What is the issue?
options: She is in a group, but not the specific group assigned to this folder

fix.q: How do you resolve this correctly?
options: Add her individual account to the folder
Add her to the 'HR_Staff' group in AD

debrief.summary: Group membership only works if the group itself has permission.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Just because a user is in 'HR' doesn't mean they automatically see every HR folder. You must verify if the specific group the user belongs to matches the group listed on the folder's security list. We add her to the group rather than adding her name directly to the folder to keep the security list clean and easy to manage.

tickets.title: USB Storage Capacity Error
tickets.summary: A user has 14GB free on a USB but can't copy a single 5GB file.

triage.q: The drive has enough space. What property should you check first?

diagnosis.q: Why does a 5GB file fail on a 16GB FAT32 volume?
options: FAT32 cannot handle any single file larger than 4GB

debrief.summary: Total space and file size limits are two different things.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You identified that the 'space available' wasn't the problem—the 'architecture' was. Even with 100GB free, a FAT32 drive will always reject a 5GB file because its 'map' isn't big enough to track a single file of that size. Switching to NTFS removes this old limitation.

tickets.title: Workstation Trust Relationship Failure
tickets.summary: A user returning from leave gets a 'trust relationship' error at login.

triage.q: What tool verifies the secure channel?

diagnosis.q: What happened while the user was away?
options: The computer's own internal password expired and fell out of sync with AD

debrief.summary: Computers have 'passwords' that expire just like users.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Computers are members of the domain too. When this laptop was off for 3 months, it missed its scheduled password rotation with Active Directory. By unjoining and rejoining, you are essentially 're-introducing' the computer to the domain so they can agree on a new secret password.

tickets.title: Folder Inheritance Discrepancy
tickets.summary: A manager created a sub-folder. The team can't see it, even though they have access to the main folder.

triage.q: How can you tell if a permission is inherited?

options: Inheritance was turned off, so the 'Allow' rules didn't 'flow down' to the new folder

debrief.summary: Permissions should flow like a waterfall from the top folder down.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: When the manager disabled inheritance, they 'broke the chain.' Even though the team had access to the top folder, the new sub-folder became a private island. Re-enabling inheritance forces the sub-folder to listen to the parent's security rules again.

tickets.title: Duplicate Computer Object Block
artifact: AD Search: 'LAPTOP-05' already exists from 2 years ago.

triage.q: Where do you check for old computer names?

options: AD is protecting the old object's identity and won't let a new machine 'clobber' it
Delete/Reset the old AD object first

debrief.summary: Active Directory remembers names to prevent security spoofing.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You found a 'stale' object. Active Directory doesn't know 'LAPTOP-05' is a brand new piece of hardware; it thinks someone is trying to impersonate an old computer. Deleting the old record clears the path for the new machine to register its own unique security ID (SID).

tickets.title: Group Conflict: The Deny Rule
tickets.summary: James is in a group that is 'Allowed' and a group that is 'Denied'. He is blocked.

options: In Windows, a 'Deny' always wins over an 'Allow'
Remove 'Deny' and leave 'Allow' unchecked for Contractors

debrief.summary: A 'Deny' is a 'No' that cannot be overruled by a 'Yes'.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You learned that 'Deny' is the most powerful setting. If you want to restrict someone, it's better to just 'not grant' them the permission. Using 'Deny' is like a master lock—even if they have a 'Yes' key from another group, the 'Deny' lock keeps the door shut.

tickets.title: Creating a New Data Partition
tickets.summary: User has a 1TB C: drive but wants a separate D: drive for projects.

debrief.summary: You can't build a new room (D:) until you clear some land (Unallocated Space).
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You can't just 'create' a D: drive if the C: drive is using the whole disk. By shrinking C:, you push the existing data to the front of the drive, leaving 'empty land' at the end where a brand new partition can be built.

tickets.title: Share vs NTFS Constraints
tickets.summary: User has Full Control on the Share but 'Read' on NTFS. They can't save files.

options: The 'Read' limit on the folder is tighter than the 'Full' limit on the share

debrief.summary: Getting through the network 'gate' is only half the battle.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Think of Share permissions as the 'security guard at the gate' and NTFS as the 'key to the office.' The guard let the user in (Full Control), but once they got to the office, their key was 'Read Only.' You have to fix the lock on the office door (NTFS) for them to do their work.

tickets.title: The Invisible Internal Drive
tickets.summary: A brand new SSD is plugged in but doesn't show in 'This PC'.

options: Needs Initialization and a Volume created

debrief.summary: A new disk is like a blank notebook with no lines or page numbers.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Windows won't show a drive until it has a 'table of contents' (Initialization) and 'pages' (Formatting). Once you initialized the disk and gave it a drive letter, you gave Windows a way to talk to the hardware.

tickets.title: Authentication Block: Time Skew
tickets.summary: Login fails. Error: 'Time difference between client and server.'

options: Security handshake fails if clocks don't match (prevents replay attacks)

debrief.summary: Security requires everyone to be on the same clock.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You identified that a 10-minute difference is too large. The domain uses time to prove that a login request is 'fresh.' If the clocks are too far apart, the server thinks someone might be trying to reuse an old, stolen login packet and blocks the access to be safe.
